1. Order of Operations (BIDMAS)
Number System
B - I - D/M - A/S
Operations must be completed in order: 1. Brackets (), 2. Indices (², ³, √), 3. Division & Multiplication (left-to-right), 4. Addition & Subtraction (left-to-right).
★ Golden Rule: Always solve brackets and powers first before multiplying or adding!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't just calculate left-to-right! 5 + 3 × 2 is 11, NOT 16.
DfE L2.N1 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
2. Negative Numbers in Context
Number System
Rules of Signs & Difference
Difference between positive & negative = Add their absolute values (|a| + |b|). Multiplying/Dividing: Same signs = POSITIVE (+). Different signs = NEGATIVE (-).
★ Golden Rule: Subtracting a negative is the same as ADDING! 5 - (-3) = 5 + 3 = 8.
⚠️ Watch Out: -5°C is COLDER than -2°C. The larger the numeral after the minus sign, the lower the value.
DfE L2.N2 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
3. Fractions, Decimals & % Equivalence
Number System
Conversion Benchmarks
To compare values, convert them all to percentages or decimals: Fraction to %: (Numerator ÷ Denominator) × 100. Decimal to %: Multiply by 100.
★ Golden Rule: Eighths are common exam traps: 1/8 = 12.5% (0.125), not 18%!
⚠️ Watch Out: 0.4 is 40%, NOT 4%! 0.04 is 4%. Count your decimal places carefully.
DfE L2.N3 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card

4. Fraction of an Amount (Non-Calc)
Number System
Divide by Bottom, Times by Top
To find a fraction (a/b) of any amount: 1. Divide total by denominator (b) to find 1 part. 2. Multiply result by numerator (a) to get required parts.
★ Golden Rule: Divide by the denominator, multiply by the numerator!
⚠️ Watch Out: If a question asks for the REMAINING amount, remember to subtract your answer from the original total.
DfE L2.N4 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
5. Adding & Subtracting Mixed Fractions
Number System
Improper & Common Denominator
1. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions (Whole × Denom + Num). 2. Find lowest common denominator (LCM). 3. Add or subtract numerators only. 4. Simplify.
★ Golden Rule: NEVER add denominators together! 1/4 + 2/3 is NEVER 3/7.
⚠️ Watch Out: When subtracting, always convert to top-heavy improper fractions first to prevent negative fractional parts.
DfE L2.N4 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
6. Multiplying & Dividing Fractions
Number System
Multiply Straight / Keep-Change-Flip
Multiplication: Multiply tops, multiply bottoms (cross-cancel if possible). Division: KEEP the first fraction, CHANGE ÷ to ×, FLIP the second fraction (reciprocal).
★ Golden Rule: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never flip the FIRST fraction — only flip the SECOND fraction after changing the sign.
DfE L2.N5 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
7. Percentage Increase & Decrease (Multiplier)
Number System
Single Multiplier Method
Increase: Add % to 100%, divide by 100. (e.g. +17.5% = × 1.175). Decrease: Subtract % from 100%, divide by 100. (e.g. -15% = × 0.85).
★ Golden Rule: Using a single multiplier is faster and eliminates rounding errors on calculator papers!
⚠️ Watch Out: Be careful with single digit percentages: +5% is × 1.05, NOT × 1.5 (which is +50%)!
DfE L2.N6 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card

8. Percentage Change Formula
Number System
(Change ÷ Original) × 100
Percentage Change = (Actual Difference ÷ Original Starting Value) × 100. Works for percentage profit, loss, discount, and inflation.
★ Golden Rule: Denominator is ALWAYS the original starting value before the change occurred!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't divide by the new price! Dividing 1,200 by 6,800 gives 17.6%, which is incorrect.
DfE L2.N7 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
9. Reverse Percentages (Original Value)
Number System
Divide by Multiplier
To find the original price before VAT or sale: 1. Identify the new percentage (e.g. Price + 20% VAT = 120% = 1.20). 2. Divide final price by multiplier (Price ÷ 1.20).
★ Golden Rule: To go BACKWARDS to the original, DIVIDE by the multiplier!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never calculate the percentage of the sale/final price and subtract! 20% of £144 is £28.80 (£115.20 = WRONG).
DfE L2.N8 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
10. Simple vs Compound Interest
Number System
Fixed Amount vs Interest on Interest
Simple: Same fixed interest paid every year. Compound: Total = Principal × (Multiplier)^Years. Interest is earned on accumulated interest.
★ Golden Rule: Compound formula: Total = Principal × (1 + r/100)ⁿ
⚠️ Watch Out: Check whether the question asks for the TOTAL ACCUMULATED AMOUNT or just the INTEREST EARNED!
DfE L2.N9 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
11. Sharing in a 3-Part Ratio
Number System
Add Parts, Divide, Multiply
1. Add all parts together to find total parts (e.g. 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts). 2. Divide total amount by total parts to find value of 1 part. 3. Multiply 1 part by each share.
★ Golden Rule: Check your work: Add the final shares together — they must equal the starting total!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't divide the total by just one number! Always sum ALL parts first.
DfE L2.N10 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card

12. Reverse Ratios (Difference / One Share)
Number System
Find 1 Part from the Difference
When told 'Person A gets £X more than Person B': 1. Find difference in ratio parts. 2. Divide given money by difference in parts = 1 part. 3. Multiply by required share.
★ Golden Rule: Match the given amount to its specific parts, NEVER the total parts!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't divide £40 by 8! The £40 represents the DIFFERENCE (2 parts), not the total.
DfE L2.N11 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
13. Direct & Inverse Proportion
Number System
Direct (Both Up) vs Inverse (One Up, One Down)
Direct: As X doubles, Y doubles (Scale factor or Unitary method). Inverse: As workers increase, time decreases! Workers × Time = Constant Total Work.
★ Golden Rule: More workers take LESS time! Multiply workers by hours to get total person-hours.
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't scale inverse proportion by multiplying both! If 3 workers take 8 hrs, 6 workers do NOT take 16 hrs!
DfE L2.N12 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
14. Best Buy & Unit Pricing
Number System
Cost per Unit (Price ÷ Quantity)
To compare value for money, find the cost for 1 unit (100g, 1ml, or 1 item): Cost per 100g = (Price in pence ÷ Grams) × 100. The lowest cost per unit is the best value.
★ Golden Rule: Convert pounds to pence first to avoid difficult decimal calculations!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't just pick the cheaper price tag — a smaller pack might cost more per 100g.
DfE L2.N13 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
15. Rounding to Significant Figures
Number System
Count from First Non-Zero Digit
1st sig fig is the first digit that is NOT zero reading left-to-right. Look at next digit: 5 or more rounds UP, 4 or less rounds DOWN. Fill trailing spaces with placeholder zeroes.
★ Golden Rule: Leading zeros in decimals NEVER count as significant figures!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't turn 48,290 into 5! You must keep the placeholder zeros (50,000).
DfE L2.N14 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card

16. Estimation & Approximation
Number System
Round Every Number to 1 Sig Fig
To estimate calculations and verify checks in Section A: Round EACH number to 1 significant figure BEFORE performing any multiplication or division.
★ Golden Rule: Dividing by 0.5 is the exact same as multiplying by 2!
⚠️ Watch Out: Do NOT calculate the exact answer first and round at the end! Examiners award zero marks if unrounded values are used.
DfE L2.N15 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
17. Powers, Roots & Indices
Number System
Square, Cube & Roots
x² = x × x. x³ = x × x × x. Square root (√x) is inverse of squaring. Cube root (∛x) is the number multiplied by itself 3 times to give x.
★ Golden Rule: 5³ is NOT 5 × 3 = 15! 5³ is 5 × 5 × 5 = 125.
⚠️ Watch Out: Square root of a number between 0 and 1 gets BIGGER! √0.25 = 0.5.
DfE L2.N16 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
18. Formula Substitution
Number System
Replace Letters with Numbers
1. Replace each variable with given numbers (use brackets around negatives!). 2. Follow BIDMAS: Multiply adjacent terms before adding. 3. Check units.
★ Golden Rule: Letters side-by-side mean MULTIPLY: 4ab means 4 × a × b!
⚠️ Watch Out: Squaring a negative number gives a positive: (-4)² = +16, NOT -16.
DfE L2.N17 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
19. Perimeter of Composite Shapes
Shape & Space
Find Missing Sides, Then Add All
1. Find every missing side: Horizontal missing side = Total width - given width. Vertical missing side = Total height - given height. 2. Sum ALL outer sides.
★ Golden Rule: Tick off each side as you add it to avoid counting sides twice or skipping one!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never add internal dotted lines when finding perimeter — perimeter is ONLY the outside border!
DfE L2.MSS18 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card

20. Circumference of a Circle
Shape & Space
Circumference = 3.142 × Diameter
Circumference is the distance around the outside edge of a circle. Diameter (d) goes straight across through center. Radius (r) is from center to edge (d = 2r).
★ Golden Rule: Distance around outside: Circumference = 3.142 × Diameter!
⚠️ Watch Out: If given radius (r), you MUST double it before multiplying by 3.142 (Diameter = 2 × r)!
DfE L2.MSS19 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
21. Area of Triangle & Parallelogram
Shape & Space
Triangle: 1/2 × b × h | Parallelogram: b × h
Both use PERPENDICULAR vertical height at 90° to the base. Triangle is halved because two identical triangles make a parallelogram/rectangle.
★ Golden Rule: Always use the perpendicular vertical height, NEVER the slanted side!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't divide by 2 for a parallelogram — only halve for a triangle!
DfE L2.MSS20 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
22. Area of a Trapezium
Shape & Space
Area = 1/2(a + b)h
1. Add parallel top and bottom sides (a + b). 2. Divide by 2 to get average parallel width. 3. Multiply by perpendicular vertical height (h).
★ Golden Rule: Half the sum of parallel sides times vertical height!
⚠️ Watch Out: Examiners include slanted side lengths as a trap. Cross out the slant immediately.
DfE L2.MSS20 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
23. Area of a Circle & Semicircle
Shape & Space
Circle: π r² = 3.142 × r² | Semicircle: (3.142 × r²) ÷ 2
The ² symbol means squared: r² means radius multiplied by itself (r × r). Calculate r² (r × r) first, then multiply by 3.142 (Area = 3.142 × r²). If given diameter, halve it first to get radius. Semicircle area is half the full circle: (3.142 × r²) ÷ 2.
★ Golden Rule: Circle Area = 3.142 × r² (where r² means Radius × Radius)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Do NOT multiply diameter by itself! Always halve diameter first to find radius.
DfE L2.MSS21 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card

24. Area of Composite Shapes
Shape & Space
Split into Simpler Shapes, Then Add
1. Split compound floor plan into non-overlapping rectangles and triangles with dashed lines. 2. Calculate area of each individual section. 3. Sum all areas.

25. Volume of Cuboids & Prisms
Shape & Space
Volume = Cross-Sectional Area × Length
A prism has the same 2D shape all the way through: 1. Find area of the front face (cross-section). 2. Multiply by the 3D length/depth. Units are cubic (cm³, m³).
★ Golden Rule: Always multiply the front face area by the full length/depth!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't confuse Volume (3D space in m³) with Surface Area (2D skin in m²).

26. Volume of a Cylinder
Shape & Space
Volume = π r² h = 3.142 × r² × h
A cylinder is a circular prism: 1. Circular base area = π r² = 3.142 × r² (where r² means r × r). 2. Multiply by vertical height (h): Volume = 3.142 × r² × h. Units are cubic (cm³, m³), where ³ means cubed (x × x × x). 1,000 cm³ = 1 Litre.
★ Golden Rule: Cylinder Volume = 3.142 × r² × h (where r² means Radius × Radius)!
⚠️ Watch Out: If given diameter, divide by 2 first to get radius! (r = d ÷ 2).
DfE L2.MSS24 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
27. Surface Area of a Cuboid
Shape & Space
SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)
A cuboid has 6 rectangular faces in 3 identical opposite pairs: 1. Front & Back (l × h) × 2. 2. Top & Bottom (l × w) × 2. 3. Left & Right (w × h) × 2. Sum all 6 faces.
★ Golden Rule: Calculate 3 faces, add them up, then multiply by 2!
⚠️ Watch Out: If painting a room, remember to EXCLUDE the floor (or ceiling and windows) if instructed!

Shape & Space

A closed cylinder net has 3 parts: Two circular ends (2 × 3.142 × r², where r² means r × r) plus one unwrapped rectangular body (3.142 × d × h).

29. Metric Unit Conversions
Shape & Space
Length, Mass & Capacity Ladders
Big unit to small unit = MULTIPLY (×). Small unit to big unit = DIVIDE (÷). Length: km (×1000) m (×100) cm (×10) mm. Mass: tonne (×1000) kg (×1000) g. Volume: L (×1000) mL.
★ Golden Rule: Kilo = 1,000 • Centi = 1/100 • Milli = 1/1,000.
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't divide 3.5 m by 100 to get cm! When going from metres to cm, you get MORE units (× 100 = 350 cm).

30. Converting Square & Cubic Units
Shape & Space
1 m² = 10,000 cm² | 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³
To convert square units, apply the linear conversion TWICE (100² = 10,000). To convert cubic units, apply conversion THREE TIMES (100³ = 1,000,000).
★ Golden Rule: Square the conversion factor for area; cube it for volume!
⚠️ Watch Out: 1 m² is NOT 100 cm²! That is the most failed unit conversion in Level 2 exams.

Core UK Benchmark Ratios

★ Golden Rule: 5 miles = 8 km. To convert km to miles, multiply by 5 then divide by 8.
⚠️ Watch Out: Kilograms are HEAVIER than pounds! 10 kg is about 22 lbs, NOT 4.5 lbs.

32. Speed, Distance & Time
Shape & Space
D = S × T | Decimal Time Warning
Distance = Speed × Time. Speed = Distance ÷ Time. Time = Distance ÷ Speed. Decimal hours must be converted: Multiply decimal minutes by 60 (0.4 hrs = 24 mins).
★ Golden Rule: Minutes to decimal: Divide by 60. Decimal to minutes: Multiply by 60.
⚠️ Watch Out: 2 hours 45 minutes on a calculator is 2.75, NEVER 2.45!

33. Density, Mass & Volume
Shape & Space
M = D × V (MDV Triangle)
Mass = Density × Volume. Density = Mass ÷ Volume (written in g/cm³ or kg/m³). Volume = Mass ÷ Density. Density measures how tightly matter is packed.
★ Golden Rule: Remember: 'Department of Motor Vehicles' (D-M-V) or Mass on top!
⚠️ Watch Out: Check units: If density is in g/cm³, volume must be in cm³ and mass must be in grams.

34. Scale Drawings & Maps
Shape & Space
Scale Ratios (1 : n)
Scale 1 : 50 means 1 cm on paper represents 50 cm in real life (0.5 m). Scale 1 : 25,000 means 1 cm = 250 m. Map to Real: MULTIPLY. Real to Map: DIVIDE.
★ Golden Rule: Both sides of a scale ratio start in the SAME unit (centimetres)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Always convert cm to metres (÷ 100) or km (÷ 100,000) for real-world answers.

Shape & Space
North • Clockwise • 3 Figures
1. Measure angle clockwise starting from North line (000°). 2. Always write using THREE digits (e.g. 045°, 090°, 260°). Back bearing = Add or subtract 180°.
★ Golden Rule: Always 3 digits! 55° must be written as 055°.
⚠️ Watch Out: Check which location the bearing is measured FROM: 'Bearing of B from A' means draw North at A!

Shape & Space
Plan View • Front • Side Elevation

37. Averages: Mean, Median, Mode & Range
Handling Data
The 4 Core Statistics
Mean = Sum of values ÷ Count. Median = Middle value after ordering low to high. Mode = Most frequent value. Range = Highest - Lowest (spread, NOT an average).
★ Golden Rule: Range is a measure of consistency/spread, NEVER an average!
⚠️ Watch Out: For the median with an even count of numbers, add the middle two and divide by 2.
DfE L2.HD34 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
38. Mean from a Frequency Table
Handling Data
Mean = Σfx ÷ Σf
1. Multiply value (x) by frequency (f) to make an fx column. 2. Sum the fx column (Total score Σfx). 3. Sum the frequency column (Total count Σf). 4. Divide: Σfx ÷ Σf.
★ Golden Rule: Divide by total frequency (Σf), NEVER by the number of rows in the table!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't just average the 'x' column — that ignores how many times each value occurred.
DfE L2.HD35 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
39. Estimated Mean (Grouped Data)
Handling Data
Midpoints × Frequency ÷ Total Frequency
1. Find midpoint of each group: (Lower bound + Upper bound) ÷ 2. 2. Multiply midpoint by frequency (mp × f). 3. Sum (mp × f). 4. Divide by total frequency.
★ Golden Rule: It is an 'ESTIMATE' because the exact individual raw values inside the group are unknown!
⚠️ Watch Out: Be careful finding midpoints: for 0 to 10, midpoint is 5. For 20 to 50, midpoint is 35 (not 30).

40. Modal Class & Median Group
Handling Data
Identifying Class Intervals
Modal Class = The group interval with the HIGHEST frequency number. Median Group = The interval that contains the middle position ((Total f + 1) ÷ 2).
★ Golden Rule: Always write the ENTIRE interval inequality (e.g. 20 < t ≤ 30), not just one number!
⚠️ Watch Out: The modal class is the interval itself, NOT the frequency count.
DfE L2.HD37 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
41. Comparing Two Data Sets
Handling Data
Average + Spread in Context
To earn full marks on Pearson comparison questions, you MUST state: 1. One Average comparison in context ('Branch A has a higher mean sales by £50'). 2. One Range/Spread comparison ('Branch B is more consistent because its range is smaller').
★ Golden Rule: Smaller range = more consistent / reliable results!
⚠️ Watch Out: Always write comparison words (higher, lower, more consistent) in context!
DfE L2.HD38 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
42. Probability of Single Events
Handling Data
P(Event) = Favourable ÷ Total
Probability is always between 0 (Impossible) and 1 (Certain). Can be written as a fraction, decimal, or percentage. P(Not event) = 1 - P(Event).
★ Golden Rule: Probabilities can NEVER be greater than 1 or negative!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't write probability as a ratio (e.g. 1 : 4 is WRONG). Write as a fraction (1/5), decimal (0.2), or % (20%).
DfE L2.HD39 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
43. Combined Independent Events
Handling Data
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
Independent events do not affect each other (e.g. flipping a coin and rolling a die). 'AND' rule = MULTIPLY probabilities. 'OR' rule = ADD probabilities.
★ Golden Rule: 'AND' means MULTIPLY; 'OR' means ADD!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't add when you need both to happen: 1/2 + 1/6 = 4/6 (which is much too high for both happening together).

44. Probability Tree Diagrams
Handling Data
Multiply Across, Add Down
1. Branches from any single node must add up to 1. 2. MULTIPLY along branches to find outcome probability. 3. ADD individual outcome probabilities together if multiple paths satisfy the question.
★ Golden Rule: Every pair of branch splits MUST add up to 1 (100%)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Check whether picking is WITH replacement or WITHOUT replacement (fractions change on 2nd pick!).
DfE L2.HD41 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
45. Two-Way Tables & Probability
Handling Data
Row Totals + Column Totals
1. Every row must add up to its row total. 2. Every column must add up to its column total. 3. Grand total bottom-right must match both row totals and column totals.
★ Golden Rule: Find the cell with only ONE missing number in its row or column first!
⚠️ Watch Out: For conditional probability ('Given that the person is a woman...'), divide by the WOMEN TOTAL (50), not the grand total (80)!
DfE L2.HD42 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
46. Scatter Diagrams & Correlation
Handling Data
Positive • Negative • Zero Correlation
Positive: As X goes up, Y goes up (slopes uphill). Negative: As X goes up, Y goes down (slopes downhill). Zero: Scattered random cloud with no trend.
★ Golden Rule: Draw a line of best fit with an equal balance of points above and below the line!
⚠️ Watch Out: Correlation does NOT prove causation! (e.g. ice cream sales and sunburn both correlate with hot weather).
DfE L2.HD43 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
47. Interpolation vs Extrapolation
Handling Data
Inside Range (Reliable) vs Beyond (Unreliable)
Interpolation: Estimating a value INSIDE the given data range (Reliable). Extrapolation: Extending line of best fit BEYOND the data points (Unreliable / Risky).
★ Golden Rule: Predictions outside the original data range are UNRELIABLE because trends may flatten or reverse!
⚠️ Watch Out: Examiners will ask 'Why might this prediction be unreliable?' — answer: 'It is extrapolated beyond the data range.'

48. Pie Charts: Angles & Frequencies
Handling Data
Angle = (Value ÷ Total) × 360°
Total degrees in any circle = 360°. Degrees per item = 360° ÷ Total Frequency. To find angle for a category: Multiply its frequency by degrees per item.
★ Golden Rule: Sum of all pie chart sector angles MUST equal exactly 360°!
⚠️ Watch Out: A pie chart only shows PROPORTIONS, not raw quantities, unless the total sample size is given!

49. Dual & Grouped Bar Charts
Handling Data
Side-by-Side Comparison with Key
Dual bar charts place two bars side-by-side for each category to compare groups (e.g. Male vs Female, 2023 vs 2024). Always check the legend key and vertical axis scale.
★ Golden Rule: Read the key carefully to avoid mixing up years or cohorts!
⚠️ Watch Out: Check the vertical axis scale increments — each grid square may represent 2, 5, 10, or 20 units.

50. Misleading Graphs & Traps
Handling Data
Non-Zero Baselines & Uneven Scales
Common tricks used to deceive: 1. Broken vertical axis (not starting at 0) exaggerates tiny differences. 2. Unequal scale increments. 3. 3D distortion making front slices look bigger.
★ Golden Rule: Always check if the vertical axis starts at ZERO (0)!
⚠️ Watch Out: A graph that looks dramatic often only represents a 1% or 2% actual difference.

2. Four Operations with Whole Numbers
Number System
Column Methods & Checking
Addition & Subtraction: Line up unit digits strictly on the right. Carry over when sum ≥ 10; borrow from next column to the left for subtraction. Multiplication: Long column. Division: Short 'bus stop'.
★ Golden Rule: Always check subtraction by adding your answer to the smaller number!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't subtract smaller from larger in the same column! If top digit is smaller, borrow 1 from left.

3. Negative Numbers (Temp & Debt)
Number System
Below Zero & Bank Overdrafts
Numbers below 0 have a minus sign (-). Moving RIGHT on the number line = getting warmer / paying in money (+). Moving LEFT = getting colder / spending money (-).
★ Golden Rule: -8°C is COLDER than -3°C!
⚠️ Watch Out: Overdraft balance: If balance is -£25 and you spend £10, new balance is -£35 (NOT -£15).
DfE L1.N3 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
4. Rounding to 10, 100, 1000
Number System
Look at the Neighbour on the Right
Find the rounding place: Look at the next digit to the right: If 5 or more (5, 6, 7, 8, 9), ROUND UP. If 4 or less (0, 1, 2, 3, 4), ROUND DOWN (stay same). Fill trailing places with 0.
★ Golden Rule: 5 to 9 climbs the vine; 0 to 4 stays on the floor!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't delete digits! When rounding 3,428 to the nearest 10, it becomes 3,430, NOT 343.
DfE L1.N4 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
5. Decimals: Place Value & Ordering
Number System
Tenths, Hundredths & Thousandths
To compare decimals: Line up decimal points vertically and pad with trailing zeros so all numbers have the same number of digits after the dot (e.g. 0.4 becomes 0.400).
★ Golden Rule: Add trailing zeroes to level the playing field before comparing decimals!
⚠️ Watch Out: 0.35 has more digits than 0.4, but 0.4 is LARGER! (0.40 > 0.35).

6. Operations with Decimals & Money
Number System
Line Up the Decimal Points
Always align the decimal points directly under each other when adding or subtracting money. Money must ALWAYS have TWO decimal places (e.g. £4.50, NEVER £4.5).
★ Golden Rule: Always write pounds with 2 decimal places: £6.20, NOT £6.2!

7. FDP Common Benchmarks
Number System
Halves, Quarters & Tenths
1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%. 1/10 = 0.1 = 10%. 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%. Memorising these visual equivalents saves time in exams.
★ Golden Rule: 1/5 is 20% (0.2), NOT 15%!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't confuse 0.1 (10%) with 0.01 (1%).
DfE L1.N7 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
8. Simplifying Fractions
Number System
Divide Top and Bottom Equally
To simplify a fraction, divide both the numerator (top) and denominator (bottom) by their Highest Common Factor (HCF). Keep dividing until no common factors remain.
★ Golden Rule: Whatever you do to the top, you MUST do to the bottom!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never subtract numbers to simplify fractions — you can ONLY divide or multiply.
DfE L1.N8 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
9. Fraction of an Amount (Basic)
Number System
Divide by Denominator, Times by Numerator
To find a unit fraction (1/n): Divide by n. To find a non-unit fraction (e.g. 3/4): 1. Divide by 4 to get 1 quarter. 2. Multiply result by 3 to get 3 quarters.
★ Golden Rule: Divide by bottom, multiply by top!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't stop after step 1! Dividing by 4 gives only ONE quarter (12 kg), you need THREE.

10. Percentages (Building Blocks)
Number System
10%, 5%, 1% Breakdown Method
Non-calculator percentage hacks: 10% = Divide by 10. 5% = Half of 10%. 1% = Divide by 100. 50% = Half (÷ 2). Combine blocks to find any percentage (e.g. 15% = 10% + 5%).
★ Golden Rule: Find 10% first — it unlocks 5%, 20%, 30%, and 15% instantly!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't divide by 15 to find 15%! You find 10% and add 5%.

11. Simple Ratios (2 Parts)
Number System
Add Parts, Divide Total, Multiply
To share £60 in ratio 1 : 3: 1. Add parts: 1 + 3 = 4 parts. 2. Divide total: £60 ÷ 4 = £15 (value of 1 part). 3. Multiply: Share 1 = £15, Share 2 = 3 × £15 = £45.
★ Golden Rule: Ratios must always be simplified to lowest whole numbers!
⚠️ Watch Out: Keep the order of the ratio correct: Person A : Person B must match the order in the text.
DfE L1.N11 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
12. Direct Proportion (Recipes)
Number System
Unitary Method: Find for 1 First
To scale a recipe: 1. Divide ingredients by the original number of servings to find the amount for 1 person. 2. Multiply by the new number of people needed.
★ Golden Rule: Find the quantity for ONE person first, then multiply!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't just add 2 to the flour because 6 is 4 + 2 — you must scale proportionally!
DfE L1.N12 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
13. Multiples, Factors & Primes
Number System
Definitions & Factor Pairs
Multiple = In the times table (Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15...). Factor = Numbers that divide in exactly with no remainder. Prime = EXACTLY two factors: 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11...).
★ Golden Rule: 1 is NOT a prime number because it only has 1 factor!
⚠️ Watch Out: Factors are smaller (or equal); multiples are larger (or equal).

Number System
Reverse Your Calculation for 1 Mark

★ Golden Rule: Use reverse operations (add ↔ subtract, multiply ↔ divide) to check!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't repeat the same sum — examiners require the inverse operation!

15. Perimeter of Rectangle & Square
Measures & Space
Add All Four Outside Edges
Perimeter is the total boundary distance around a 2D shape. Rectangle: Perimeter = Length + Width + Length + Width = 2l + 2w. Units are linear (cm, m).
★ Golden Rule: Perimeter is the border fence around the shape!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't just add 8 + 5 = 13! A rectangle has FOUR sides, so you must add all 4 sides.

16. Perimeter of Regular Polygons
Measures & Space
Side Length × Number of Sides
A 'regular' polygon has sides that are ALL EQUAL in length: Equilateral Triangle = 3 × side. Pentagon = 5 × side. Hexagon = 6 × side. Octagon = 8 × side.
★ Golden Rule: Regular means all sides and angles are identical!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't count the sides incorrectly: Hexagon = 6, Octagon = 8, Pentagon = 5.

Measures & Space
Area = Length × Width
Area measures the flat 2D space inside a shape. Multiply length by width. Answers are ALWAYS written in square units (cm², m², mm²).
★ Golden Rule: Area is flat surface (carpet/grass), measured in square units (m²)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't confuse Area (L × W) with Perimeter (L + W + L + W).

25. Properties of 2D Shapes
Measures & Space
Sides, Angles & Symmetry
Right Angle = 90°. Triangle angles sum to 180°. Quadrilateral angles sum to 360°. Parallel lines never meet. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.
★ Golden Rule: All angles in ANY triangle add up to 180°!
⚠️ Watch Out: A rhombus has 4 equal sides, but its angles are NOT 90° (a square has 90° angles).

26. Properties of 3D Solids
Measures & Space
Faces, Edges & Vertices
Face = Flat or curved surface. Edge = Line where two faces meet. Vertex (Vertices) = Corner point where edges meet. A cube/cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.
★ Golden Rule: Vertices = Corners • Edges = Creases • Faces = Surfaces.
⚠️ Watch Out: A cylinder has 3 faces (2 flat circles, 1 curved), 2 edges, and 0 vertices!

27. Coordinates (x, y)
Measures & Space
Along the Corridor, Up the Stairs
Coordinates are written as (x, y): 1. First number (x) goes HORIZONTALLY along the bottom axis. 2. Second number (y) goes VERTICALLY up the side axis. Origin is (0, 0).
★ Golden Rule: 'x' comes before 'y' in the alphabet, and in coordinates (x, y)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't mix up (2, 5) with (5, 2) — always read the bottom horizontal axis first.

28. Scale Drawings on Grid Paper
Measures & Space
Count Squares & Use the Key
Always check the scale key (e.g. 1 square = 1 metre, or 1 square = 2 metres). Real dimension = Number of squares counted × Scale key value.
★ Golden Rule: Always read the scale key: 1 square is rarely 1 cm in real life!
⚠️ Watch Out: If 1 square = 2 metres, 4 squares = 8 metres, NOT 4 metres.

29. Mean Average (Step-by-Step)
Handling Data
Add All Up, Divide by Count
1. Add all numbers together to find total sum. 2. Count how many numbers there are. 3. Divide total sum by the count. Mean is the fair share.
★ Golden Rule: Divide by how many items you added up!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't forget to press equals (=) before dividing on your calculator, or use brackets.

30. Median (Middle Value)
Handling Data
Line Up Low to High, Pick Middle
1. Put numbers in numerical order from smallest to largest. 2. Cross off one from each end until you reach the middle number. If two remain in middle, find their midpoint.
★ Golden Rule: You MUST sort the numbers from smallest to largest first!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never pick the middle number of the unsorted list (in 9, 3, 7, 2, 8, '7' happens to be middle, but never rely on luck!).
DfE L1.HD29 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
31. Mode (Most Frequent)
Handling Data
The Most Common Item
Mode is the number or category that appears MOST OFTEN in the data. There can be one mode, more than one mode (bimodal), or no mode if all values appear once.
★ Golden Rule: 'MO'de = 'MO'st often!
⚠️ Watch Out: The mode can be words (e.g. Blue, Coffee) — it is the only average that works for non-numbers.
DfE L1.HD30 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
32. Range (Spread of Data)
Handling Data
Range = Highest - Lowest
Range is NOT an average — it measures how spread out the numbers are. Subtract the smallest number from the largest number. Smaller range = more consistent.
★ Golden Rule: Range = Highest minus Lowest!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't write '12 to 25' — the range is a SINGLE number obtained by subtracting (13).
DfE L1.HD31 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
33. Tally Charts & Frequency
Handling Data
Bundles of 5 (4 Vertical + 1 Diagonal Gate)
Tallies are grouped in bundles of five: four vertical marks (||||) with the fifth mark crossing diagonally as a gate across the bundle. Frequency is the total count written as a number.
★ Golden Rule: The 5th tally stroke always gates diagonally across the bundle of 4!
⚠️ Watch Out: Check your raw data twice by crossing off each item as you record its tally mark.

34. Bar Charts & Scales
Handling Data
Equal Widths, Equal Gaps, Labelled Axes
To draw a bar chart for full marks: 1. Evenly spaced linear scale on vertical axis starting at 0. 2. Label both axes (e.g. 'Days' and 'Frequency'). 3. Equal width bars with equal gaps between them.
★ Golden Rule: Bars must NOT touch each other in a categorical bar chart!
⚠️ Watch Out: Check what 1 grid square represents on the vertical axis (e.g. 1 square might be 2 or 5 units).

35. Pictograms (Using a Key)
Handling Data
Always Check the Symbol Key
A pictogram uses pictures or symbols to represent quantities. Look at the key: 1 whole symbol = n items. A half symbol = n ÷ 2. A quarter symbol = n ÷ 4.
★ Golden Rule: Always check the KEY first — one picture is rarely just 1 item!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't count the number of symbols without multiplying by the key value.
DfE L1.HD34 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
36. Line Graphs (Trends over Time)
Handling Data
Plot Points & Join with Straight Lines
Line graphs show how continuous data changes over time (temperature, sales, patient heart rate). Time is plotted along the horizontal axis. Read points by looking across to vertical axis.
★ Golden Rule: Time always goes along the bottom horizontal axis!
⚠️ Watch Out: Join the plotted data points with neat straight ruler lines from point to point.
DfE L1.HD35 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
37. Probability Words & Scale
Handling Data
Impossible to Certain
0 = Impossible (can never happen). 0.5 (1/2 or 50%) = Even Chance (e.g. flipping heads). 1 = Certain (guaranteed to happen). Unlikely is between 0 and 0.5; Likely is between 0.5 and 1.
★ Golden Rule: Probabilities on a number scale run strictly from 0 to 1!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't use words like 'Good chance' or 'Fifty-fifty' on an exam — use 'Likely' or 'Even chance'.

1. Identifying Text Purpose
Reading & Analysis
P.A.F: Purpose • Audience • Form
Every text has a primary purpose: Persuade (sway opinions), Inform (factual details), Instruct (step-by-step directions), Explain (how/why something works), Advise (recommendations), or Entertain.
★ Golden Rule: Pair purpose with evidence (e.g. 'persuades via rhetorical questions').
⚠️ Watch Out: Identify the main purpose first — secondary intentions come second.
DfE L2.R1 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
2. Audience & Tone Adaptation
Reading & Analysis
Who is the Reader?
Authors adapt their language, register, and layout for specific demographics: Professionals (formal jargon), Teenagers (casual, modern idioms), Parents, Patients, Customers.
★ Golden Rule: Determine audience by looking at formality, vocabulary, and pronouns.
⚠️ Watch Out: Avoid vague labels like 'general public' — name the exact audience.
DfE L2.R2 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
3. Explicit vs Implicit (Inference)
Reading & Analysis
Fact Stated vs Reading Between Lines
Explicit = Directly and openly stated in the text word-for-word. Implicit = Hinted or suggested through clues, tone, and connotations without being said outright.
★ Golden Rule: Inference = Clues from text + Reader's logical deductions!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't guess wild theories — every inference MUST be grounded in textual clues.

4. Fact vs Opinion vs Bias
Reading & Analysis
Verifiable Truth vs Subjective Belief
Fact: Can be proven true or false with objective evidence or data. Opinion: A personal view, feeling, or judgment. Bias: A one-sided presentation favouring one perspective.
★ Golden Rule: If it contains adjectives like 'finest', 'dreadful', or 'unacceptable', it is an OPINION!
⚠️ Watch Out: Watch out for opinions disguised as facts: 'Everyone knows London is the best city' is STILL an opinion.
DfE L2.R4 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
5. Organisational Features & Effects
Reading & Analysis
Subheadings, Sidebars & Bullet Points
Always explain WHY an organisational feature is used: Subheadings (break text into chunks), Bullet points (isolate key items), Bold text (draws eye to essential warnings), Tables (organise data).
★ Golden Rule: Always explain HOW the feature guides the reader (not just its name)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Say 'draws reader's eye to safety steps', never just 'looks nice'.
DfE L2.R5 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
6. Structural Signposting
Reading & Analysis
Chronological • Cause-Effect • Problem-Solution
Structure is how the writer organizes their points over time: Problem-Solution, Cause-and-Effect, Chronological narrative, or Thematic. Look for discourse markers (Firstly, Conversely, Therefore).
★ Golden Rule: Track shifts in topic and tone from opening to conclusion!
⚠️ Watch Out: Structure means the ORDER and flow of ideas — not spelling or grammar.
DfE L2.R6 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
7. Persuasive Devices (DAFOREST)
Reading & Analysis
The Master Persuasion Toolkit
D - Direct Address ('you'). A - Alliteration. F - Facts. O - Opinions. R - Rhetorical questions. E - Emotive language. S - Statistics (85%). T - Rule of Three (triples).
★ Golden Rule: Quote the exact phrase, name the DAFOREST device, and explain how it influences the reader!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't just write 'it makes you want to read on' — explain that it creates guilt, urgency, or authority.

8. Figurative Language Devices
Reading & Analysis
Metaphor • Simile • Hyperbole
Simile: Compares using 'like' or 'as' ('busy as a bee'). Metaphor: States one thing IS another ('the hospital was a warzone'). Hyperbole: Deliberate dramatic exaggeration.
★ Golden Rule: Metaphors create vivid mental images by transferring qualities from one concept to another!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't confuse similes and metaphors: similes use 'like' or 'as'; metaphors do not.

9. Analysing Tone and Register
Reading & Analysis
The Writer's Attitude & Mood
Tone is the emotion or attitude behind the words: Sarcastic, Urgent, Critical, Humorous, Sympathetic, Objective, or Authoritative. Proved by diction (choice of words).
★ Golden Rule: Use precise tone adjectives instead of basic words like 'happy' or 'angry'!
⚠️ Watch Out: Tone can change within a text — look at the overall prevailing attitude.
DfE L2.R9 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
10. Comparing Purpose & Perspective
Reading & Analysis
Pearson Section B Master Technique
To compare two texts for top marks: 1. Identify where both authors agree or share common ground. 2. Contrast how their viewpoints differ. 3. Use comparative connectives ('In contrast', 'Similarly').
★ Golden Rule: Always refer to BOTH Text A and Text B in every comparative paragraph!
⚠️ Watch Out: Writing two separate summaries without comparing them will cost you half the marks.

Reading & Analysis
Visual Presentation Differences
Contrast the presentation: Text A may use formal paragraph blocks and footnotes, whereas Text B uses subheadings, bullet points, callout boxes, and bold text.
★ Golden Rule: Link the layout choice to how it helps the intended reader navigate the text!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't just mention font colours unless it specifically relates to emphasis or branding.

13. Evaluating Source Credibility
Reading & Analysis
Authority • Date • Vested Interest
To evaluate reliability: 1. Author authority (doctor vs blogger). 2. Publication date (is it outdated?). 3. Commercial bias (is the writer selling a product?). 4. Corroboration (can claims be verified?).
★ Golden Rule: Sources with commercial or personal interests are likely biased!
⚠️ Watch Out: Check author credentials — official-looking sites can still be biased.

14. Specialist Vocabulary & Jargon
Reading & Analysis
Deduce Meaning from Context
When encountering unfamiliar technical terms or jargon: 1. Read the surrounding sentences for clues. 2. Break down prefixes and root words. 3. Substitute a synonym to check if it makes sense.
★ Golden Rule: Use surrounding sentences to deduce the meaning of unfamiliar terms!
⚠️ Watch Out: Look for definitions nearby — don't skip technical terms.

15. Main Ideas vs Supporting Details
Reading & Analysis
Core Claim vs Examples
Main Idea: The central argument or topic sentence of a paragraph. Supporting Details: Statistics, quotes, illustrative anecdotes, and examples that prove the main claim.
★ Golden Rule: The topic sentence at the start of a paragraph usually states the main idea!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't mistake a single supporting case study for the writer's overarching point.

16. Summarising Multiple Paragraphs
Reading & Analysis
Synthesise in Your Own Words

★ Golden Rule: Exams penalise mindless copying — rewording proves you understood the text!
⚠️ Watch Out: Leave out minor descriptive details, anecdotes, and redundant adjectives.

17. Irony, Satire & Sarcasm
Reading & Analysis
Saying the Opposite of What is Meant
Verbal Irony: When an author says the opposite of their true meaning for humorous or critical effect. Understatement: Deliberately minimising seriousness ('it's just a scratch' on a wrecked car).
★ Golden Rule: Check if praise is sincere or sarcastic by looking at the broader context!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't take ironic statements literally — that leads to picking the exact opposite answer.

18. Golden Reading Method: Q-E-L
Reading & Analysis
Quote • Explain • Link
To score full marks on 3-mark and 4-mark reading questions: 1. QUOTE exact textual phrase in quotation marks. 2. EXPLAIN the underlying meaning in your own words. 3. LINK directly to the author's purpose or question.
★ Golden Rule: Keep quotes short (1 to 5 words) — never copy entire three-line sentences!
⚠️ Watch Out: A quote without explanation earns 0 or 1 mark; you must explain its impact.

★ Golden Rule: Named = Yours sincerely; Unnamed (Dear Sir/Madam) = Yours faithfully!

Hook • Context • Thesis Statement

Writing & Formats
Re-state • Synthesise • Final Call
Never introduce brand new arguments in a conclusion! 1. Restate your main stance in fresh words. 2. Synthesise your strongest arguments. 3. End with a memorable final call to action or warning.
★ Golden Rule: Leave the examiner with a punchy, lingering final sentence!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never bring up brand-new evidence in the conclusion — it looks unplanned.

Writing & Formats
Linking Ideas Across Paragraphs

★ Golden Rule: Put a comma immediately after fronted connective words (e.g. 'Furthermore, ...')!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't overuse 'Also', 'And', or 'But' to start every sentence.

★ Golden Rule: Follow fronted openers with a comma to separate the clause!
⚠️ Watch Out: A piece where every sentence begins with 'The' or 'We' feels monotonous and loses grammar marks.

Writing & Formats
Swap Weak Words for Sophisticated Diction

33. Planning & Proofreading Strategy
Writing & Formats
5-Minute Plan • Write • 5-Minute Sweep
Time allocation strategy: 5 mins: Spidergram plan (format, 4 key points, PAF). 35 mins: Sustained writing following PEEL. 5 mins: Proofreading sweep for capital letters, sentence boundaries, and homophones.
★ Golden Rule: Plan for 5 minutes and reserve 5 minutes at the end to proofread!
⚠️ Watch Out: Always proofread — catching 3 SPaG errors can make or break a pass.

34. Sentence Boundaries & Splices
SPaG & Grammar
Never Join Sentences with a Comma Alone
A comma splice occurs when two independent sentences are joined with only a comma. Fix it with: 1. A full stop. 2. A semicolon (;). 3. A coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
★ Golden Rule: A comma is a brief pause, NEVER a full stop!
⚠️ Watch Out: Comma splices are the #1 penalized grammar error at Level 2.
DfE L2.W34 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
35. The Comma Rulebook
SPaG & Grammar
Lists • Adverbials • Parenthetical Clauses
Use commas for: 1. Separating items in a list. 2. After introductory adverbials ('Suddenly, ...'). 3. Around non-essential parenthetical information ('Dr Smith, who retired last year, attended').
★ Golden Rule: Use commas after fronted adverbials and around non-essential clauses!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never insert a comma between a subject and its main verb.

36. Apostrophes: Omission vs Possession
SPaG & Grammar
Missing Letters vs Ownership
Omission: Replaces missing letters in contractions (don't = do not, it's = it is). Singular possession: 's (the nurse's badge). Plural ending in s: s' (the nurses' station). Irregular plural: 's (children's ward).
★ Golden Rule: 'Its' for possession NEVER has an apostrophe (like hers, his, ours)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never use an apostrophe to make a word plural! (e.g. 'Apple's for sale' is WRONG).
DfE L2.W36 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
37. Colons & Semicolons
SPaG & Grammar
Colon (Introduces) • Semicolon (Bridges)
Colon (:): Introduces a list, explanation, or direct quotation following a full independent clause. Semicolon (;): Connects two closely linked independent sentences without a conjunction.
★ Golden Rule: The clause before a colon MUST be a complete standalone sentence!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't put a colon after a verb like 'including' or 'are' (e.g. 'Items are: pen...' is INCORRECT).
DfE L2.W37 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
38. Speech Marks & Quotations
SPaG & Grammar
Punctuation Inside the Quotes
1. Put quotation marks around the spoken words only. 2. Punctuation (comma, full stop, exclamation mark) goes INSIDE the speech marks. 3. New speaker = start a new paragraph line.
★ Golden Rule: Punctuation belongs INSIDE the speech marks!
⚠️ Watch Out: Capitalise the first word inside the opening speech mark when starting dialogue.
DfE L2.W38 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
39. Hyphens & Parenthetical Dashes
SPaG & Grammar
Hyphen (Joins) vs Dash (Separates)
Hyphen (-): Short line joining words to form compound adjectives before nouns (well-known actor, part-time job). Dash (—): Longer pause used in pairs for dramatic emphasis or parenthetical side-thoughts.
★ Golden Rule: Hyphens glue words together; dashes push thoughts apart!
⚠️ Watch Out: Notice the difference: 'twenty five-pound notes' (20 notes) vs 'twenty-five pound notes' (£25 notes).

40. Subject-Verb Agreement
SPaG & Grammar
Singular Subjects take Singular Verbs
Singular subject = singular verb (The student IS writing). Plural subject = plural verb (The students ARE writing). Trap: Ignore prepositional phrases (e.g. 'The box of chocolates IS on the desk').
★ Golden Rule: Singular subjects take singular verbs (he runs; they run)!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'Everyone', 'each', and 'nobody' always take SINGULAR verbs.
DfE L2.W40 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
41. Consistent Verb Tenses
SPaG & Grammar
Maintain Tense Throughout
Do not drift accidentally between past and present tense within the same sentence or paragraph: Reports and recount narratives must stay strictly in the past tense.
★ Golden Rule: Check all your verbs during proofreading to ensure they match in tense!
⚠️ Watch Out: Accidental tense drift into present tense is common when writing recount stories.
DfE L2.W41 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
42. Active vs Passive Voice
SPaG & Grammar
Active (Direct) vs Passive (Formal & Objective)
Active: Subject performs action ('The doctor administered the vaccine'). Direct and energetic. Passive: Action happens to subject ('The vaccine was administered'). Formal, impersonal, ideal for reports.
★ Golden Rule: Use active voice ('We improved...') for clear, direct writing!
⚠️ Watch Out: Overusing passive voice creates sluggish, bureaucratic sentences.
DfE L2.W42 • Level 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
43. Complex & Compound Sentences
SPaG & Grammar
Main Clauses & Subordinate Clauses
Compound: Joins two independent clauses with FANBOYS conjunction (and, but, so). Complex: Contains a main clause + subordinate clause joined with subordinating conjunction (although, because, while, since).
★ Golden Rule: When a subordinate clause comes first, always put a comma after it!
⚠️ Watch Out: A subordinate clause alone is a fragment, NOT a complete sentence.

44. Homophones: There / Their / They're
SPaG & Grammar
Location • Ownership • Contraction
THERE: Place or fact ('Put it over there', 'There is a problem'). THEIR: Ownership / belonging ('Their coats'). THEY'RE: Short for 'they are' ('They're leaving now').
★ Golden Rule: If you can replace it with 'they are', use 'they're'!
⚠️ Watch Out: Affect vs Effect: Affect is a Verb (Action), Effect is a Noun (End result).

45. Confusable Pairs: Practice vs Practise
SPaG & Grammar
Noun (C) vs Verb (S)
In British English: Nouns end in 'ce' (Practice, Advice, Device, Licence). Verbs end in 'se' (Practise, Advise, Devise, License). Tip: Think of 'Ice is a noun' (-ice = noun).
★ Golden Rule: Test with 'Advice/Advise': You give advice (noun), you advise someone (verb)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Loose vs Lose: 'Loose' rhymes with goose (untied shoelace). 'Lose' has one 'o' (to misplace something).

46. Suffix Rules (-able vs -ible)
SPaG & Grammar
Root Word Test
-able: Used when the base word is a complete standalone word (depend → dependable, enjoy → enjoyable). -ible: Used when the base word is not a complete English word (horr → horrible, vis → visible).
★ Golden Rule: If you take away the suffix and have a complete word left, use -able!
⚠️ Watch Out: -tion vs -sion: Use -sion when base word ends in d/s (extend → extension; divide → division).

The 10 Most Common Exam Misspellings
1. Accommodate (2 c's, 2 m's). 2. Definitely (de-finite-ly, NO 'a'). 3. Necessary (1 collar, 2 socks: 1 c, 2 s's). 4. Government (has 'n'). 5. Environment (has 'n'). 6. Colleague. 7. Separate.
★ Golden Rule: Break tricky words into syllables or mnemonics!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'Definately' is always marked wrong — remember 'definitely'.

48. Prefixes & Negative Antonyms
SPaG & Grammar
Un-, In-, Im-, Dis-, Mis-, Ir-
Prefixes change word meaning without altering base word spelling: 'im-' before 'p/m' (patient → impatient). 'ir-' before 'r' (responsible → irresponsible). 'il-' before 'l' (legal → illegal). Root spelling is PRESERVED.
★ Golden Rule: Don't drop letters when adding prefixes: un + necessary = unnecessary (keep both n's)!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'Disappointed' has ONE 's' and TWO 'p's (dis + appoint + ed).

49. SLC L2: Structuring a Formal Presentation
Speaking & Listening
Hook • 3 Evidence Pillars • Rebuttal • Q&A
A Level 2 presentation (5–8 mins + Q&A) requires: (1) Engaging Hook & Thesis, (2) 3 Structured Pillars supported by real statistics/examples, (3) Counter-Argument rebuttal, and (4) Call to Action.
★ Golden Rule: Rule of 3: Outline your points, present them, then summarise clearly!
⚠️ Watch Out: Pause after key ideas — rushing through costs presentation marks.

50. SLC L2: Defending Points in Q&A
Speaking & Listening
Acknowledge • Evidence • Connect (A-E-C)
When challenged in Q&A, use A-E-C: (1) Acknowledge the question calmly, (2) Explain with specific evidence or a practical example, and (3) Conclude by linking back to your main proposal.
★ Golden Rule: Never give a one-sentence answer in Level 2 Q&A—always cite evidence!
⚠️ Watch Out: Becoming defensive or saying "I don't know" without offering a reasoned response loses marks.

Speaking & Listening
Formal Register vs Collaborative Discussion
Level 2 requires adapting spoken register to your audience and purpose: use formal discourse markers ("Consequently", "Furthermore") and specialist terminology in presentations, and collaborative warmth in peer discussions.
★ Golden Rule: Adapt vocabulary and formality to match professional discussions!
⚠️ Watch Out: Avoid slang terms ('gonna', 'cheers') during formal assessments.

52. SLC L2: Mediating & Reaching Consensus
Speaking & Listening
Synthesise • Mediate • Steer to Consensus
To excel in the Level 2 formal discussion (15 mins): synthesise different viewpoints, mediate disagreements constructively, challenge assumptions with evidence, and help steer the group to a shared conclusion.
★ Golden Rule: Acknowledge opposing views fairly before proposing a compromise!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never dismiss arguments outright — validate before reframing.

1. Main Points and Ideas
Reading Skills
What is the Big Picture?
The main point is the most important message the author wants you to understand. Read the title, opening sentence, and closing sentence to identify the central message.
★ Golden Rule: The main point is the overarching message, NOT a small illustrative detail!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't confuse an example with the main point.

2. Text Types: Inform, Persuade, Instruct
Reading Skills
Identify the Goal
Inform: Gives facts and data (news, timetables). Persuade: Wants you to buy or believe something (adverts, flyers). Instruct: Tells you how to do something step-by-step (recipes, user guides).
★ Golden Rule: Look for imperative verbs (Chop, Turn, Press) = INSTRUCT!
⚠️ Watch Out: Adverts inform you about prices, but their PRIMARY goal is to PERSUADE you to buy.

Reading Skills
Signposts for Quick Navigation
Main Heading: Tells you what the whole document is about. Subheadings: Break the text into topics so you can quickly scan and find specific details without reading every single word.
★ Golden Rule: Read the subheadings first to find where your answer is hiding!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't read the whole article line-by-line if a subheading tells you exactly where the topic is.

Reading Skills
Clear, Distinct Items
Bullet points: Separate key items in a list so they stand out clearly. Numbered lists: Indicate a strict order of steps that must be done in sequence (1st, 2nd, 3rd).

Reading Skills
Visual Evidence & Explanations
Images and diagrams reinforce the written text. Captions are the short descriptive sentences directly below an image explaining what it shows.
★ Golden Rule: Always read the small print in the caption — it often contains exam answers!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't ignore the pictures — exam questions often ask how the graphic supports the article.

6. Fact vs Opinion (Core Test)
Reading Skills
True / False vs Personal Belief
Fact: Can be proven true with dates, measurements, or official records ('The shop opens at 8 am'). Opinion: What someone thinks or feels ('The shop is wonderful').
★ Golden Rule: If it uses words like 'best', 'delicious', or 'terrible', it is an OPINION!
⚠️ Watch Out: Numbers and dates are almost always facts.

7. Skimming for Overall Gist
Reading Skills
Rapid 30-Second Glance
Skimming is fast reading to get the general idea: 1. Read the title and subheadings. 2. Glance at the first and last sentence of each paragraph. 3. Look at any pictures. Do NOT read every word.
★ Golden Rule: Skimming gives you the big picture without getting bogged down!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't read word-by-word when skimming — keep your eyes moving quickly down the page.

8. Scanning for Facts & Numbers
Reading Skills
Search like a Metal Detector
Scanning is searching for specific targets: Look for capital letters (names, places), numbers (dates, times, prices), or symbols (£, %, @). Ignore everything else until you spot your target.
★ Golden Rule: Lock your target in your mind before your eyes touch the page!

9. Simple Inference (Reading Clues)
Reading Skills
Detective Reading
Inference means working out meaning from hints in the text: If someone is wearing a heavy winter coat, gloves, and shivering, you infer that the weather is freezing.
★ Golden Rule: Inference is finding the hidden clue in the writer's description!
⚠️ Watch Out: Make sure your answer is directly supported by words in the text.

10. Vocabulary: Using Context Clues
Reading Skills
Guess the Word from the Sentence
If you don't know a word: 1. Read the words before and after it. 2. Look for examples or explanations in the sentence. 3. Try replacing it with a word you do know that makes sense.
★ Golden Rule: Read the whole sentence before deciding an unknown word is impossible!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't panic when you see long words — look for root words you already recognise.

Dictionaries & Index Pages

★ Golden Rule: Look at the 3rd and 4th letter if the first two letters are identical!
⚠️ Watch Out: Surnames in directories are listed Last Name first: 'Smith, John'.

12. Instructions & Step-by-Step
Reading Skills
Chronological Sequence & Imperatives
Instructions must be followed in order. Look for sequence words: First, Next, Then, After that, Finally. Action verbs (bossy verbs) start each instruction ('Turn off power').
★ Golden Rule: Instructions always use imperative 'bossy' verbs at the start of sentences!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never skip a step when answering questions about instructional texts.

13. Formal vs Informal Language
Reading Skills
Professional vs Casual Speech
Formal: Used with managers, council, doctors ('I am writing to enquire', no slang, full words). Informal: Used with friends, family ('Hi mate', contractions, emojis, casual phrases).
★ Golden Rule: Avoid contractions (don't, can't) when writing formal letters or reports!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't use informal slang like 'gonna' or 'cool' in workplace emails.

14. Comparing Two Simple Texts
Reading Skills
What is the Same? What is Different?
To compare two texts at Level 1: 1. State one piece of information that BOTH texts agree on. 2. State one difference between the two texts (e.g. price, opening time, or opinion).
★ Golden Rule: Always answer both parts: one similarity AND one difference!
⚠️ Watch Out: Make sure you name both Text A and Text B in your answer.

15. Target Audience (Who is it for?)
Reading Skills
Spotting Who the Text is Written For
To find the audience, look at who benefits from the information: Parents (school notices), Motorists (parking leaflet), Dog owners, Job seekers, Patients.
★ Golden Rule: Be specific when naming the audience (e.g. 'Gym members', NOT just 'adults')!

20. Writing an Event Flyer / Leaflet
Writing Skills
Who • What • Where • When • Cost
A flyer must include the 5 W's: What the event is. When (date & time). Where (venue). Cost (ticket price / free). Who to contact (email / telephone / website).
★ Golden Rule: Make dates, times, and venue stand out with bullet points!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't forget contact details — visitors need to know how to book or ask questions.

Writing Skills
What You Liked & What Could Improve
Review structure: 1. Star rating (e.g. 4/5). 2. What you bought or experienced. 3. Positive features. 4. One thing that could be improved. 5. Overall recommendation.
★ Golden Rule: Give specific reasons for your opinion rather than just saying 'it was good'!
⚠️ Watch Out: Mention both pros and at least one small con to show balanced judgment.

Writing Skills
Strictly Factual & Clear

★ Golden Rule: Incident reports must be 100% factual — state only what happened!

New Idea = New Paragraph

★ Golden Rule: Leave a clear blank line between paragraphs in your exam!

24. Using Linking Connectives
Writing Skills
Joining Sentences Smoothly
Use connectives to connect ideas: Adding (and, also, as well as). Contrasting (but, however, although). Explaining cause (because, so, therefore). Sequencing (then, after that, finally).
★ Golden Rule: Linking words turn short choppy sentences into flowing prose!

Writing Skills
Start with Imperative Verbs
When writing instructions, start each point with a clear command verb (imperative): 'Chop', 'Wash', 'Turn', 'Press', 'Check'. Keep sentences direct, short, and numbered.
★ Golden Rule: Put the action verb first: 'Press button', not 'You should press button'!
⚠️ Watch Out: Avoid polite padding like 'If you wouldn't mind pressing...' in user instructions.

Writing Skills
Mix Short and Long Sentences
Use a mix: Short sentences create impact, suspense, or clarity ('Stop immediately.'). Longer compound sentences explain reasons and add detail smoothly.
★ Golden Rule: A short sentence at the end of a paragraph creates drama and punch!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't write endless rambling sentences joined by 'and... and... and...'.

Writing Skills
Professional Courtesy

★ Golden Rule: Polite firmness achieves faster results than angry hostility!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never write in ALL CAPITALS in an email — it looks like shouting.

28. Proofreading Checklist
Writing Skills
Final 3-Minute Sweep
Before submitting: 1. Capitals on names and 'I'. 2. Full stop at every sentence end. 3. Correct homophones (there/their/they're). 4. Clear paragraphs. 5. Does every sentence make sense?
★ Golden Rule: Read your work slowly in your head to check for missing words!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't rush to finish early — use the last minutes to collect easy SPaG marks.

29. Capital Letters: 5 Golden Rules
SPaG Essentials
M.I.N.T.S Rules
Always use a capital letter for: M - Months & Days (Monday, July). I - The word 'I'. N - Names of people & places (Sarah, London). T - Titles of books/films. S - Start of every sentence.
★ Golden Rule: The word 'I' is ALWAYS a capital letter, no matter where it is in a sentence!
⚠️ Watch Out: Days and months must have capitals: 'wednesday' and 'august' are WRONG.

30. Full Stops & Question Marks
SPaG Essentials
Sentence Endings
Every complete sentence must end with an end mark: Full stop (.) for statements. Question mark (?) for direct questions starting with Who, What, Where, When, Why, How, or Can.
★ Golden Rule: Direct questions always demand a question mark (?)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never use multiple question marks (???) or full stops (...!) in exam writing.

SPaG Essentials
Urgency, Surprise & Warning
Use exclamation marks (!) sparingly to show strong emotion, surprise, danger, or urgency ('Watch out!', 'What wonderful news!'). Avoid in formal letters and reports.
★ Golden Rule: One exclamation mark is enough — never write '!!' or '!!!'!
⚠️ Watch Out: Overusing exclamation marks makes writing look childish.

32. Commas in Lists
SPaG Essentials
Separating 3 or More Items
Use commas to separate items in a list of three or more things. Do NOT put a comma before the word 'and' at the end of a simple list.
★ Golden Rule: Comma between items, 'and' before the final item!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't put a comma after the final item in the list.
DfE L1.W32 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
33. Apostrophes for Contractions
SPaG Essentials
Replacing Missing Letters
An apostrophe replaces missing letters when two words are joined into one: do not → don't (o is missing). cannot → can't (no is missing). it is → it's (i is missing).
★ Golden Rule: The apostrophe sits exactly where the missing letter used to be!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't write 'dont' or 'cant' without an apostrophe — examiners mark these as spelling errors.
DfE L1.W33 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
34. Apostrophes for Possession
SPaG Essentials
Showing Who Owns What
Singular owner: Add 's after the owner's name (the boy's bike = bike belongs to one boy). Plural owners: If word already ends in s, just add apostrophe after the s (the boys' bikes = bikes belong to many boys).
★ Golden Rule: Ask: 'Who does it belong to?' Then put the apostrophe after the owner!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'CDs' and '1990s' do NOT have apostrophes (they are simple plurals).
DfE L1.W34 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
35. Plural Spelling Rules
SPaG Essentials
-s, -es, -ies, -ves
Standard: Add -s (book → books). Ending in ch, sh, s, x: Add -es (box → boxes, watch → watches). Ending in consonant + y: Drop y, add -ies (baby → babies). Ending in f/fe: Change to -ves (leaf → leaves).
★ Golden Rule: If there's a vowel before 'y' (boy, day), just add 's' (boys, days)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't write 'babys' or 'boxs' — apply the rules.

36. Irregular Plurals
SPaG Essentials
Words That Change Internally
Some words change their internal vowels instead of adding 's': man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, tooth → teeth, foot → feet, mouse → mice. Sheep and fish stay the same.
★ Golden Rule: Never add an 's' to irregular plurals: 'childrens' is WRONG!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'Women' is pronounced 'wim-in' (plural); 'woman' is singular.

37. Subject-Verb Agreement (L1)
SPaG Essentials
Singular vs Plural Matching
I go / He goes. We are / She is. They were / He was. You do / She does. The verb must agree with who is doing the action.
★ Golden Rule: 'We was' is always marked wrong — it must be 'We were'!
⚠️ Watch Out: Watch out for slang habits in speaking that creep into written work.
DfE L1.W37 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
38. Past Tense (-ed Rules)
SPaG Essentials
Regular Past Tense Suffixes
Most regular verbs add -ed (walk → walked). If verb ends in 'e', just add 'd' (like → liked). If short vowel + consonant, double consonant (stop → stopped, plan → planned).
★ Golden Rule: Double the consonant if the vowel before it is short (hop → hopped)!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'Hoped' (from hope) has one 'p'; 'hopped' (from hop) has two 'p's.
DfE L1.W38 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
39. Irregular Past Tense Verbs
SPaG Essentials
Saw • Went • Bought • Came
Irregular verbs do NOT add -ed in the past tense: See → saw (NOT seened or sawed). Go → went (NOT goed). Buy → bought (NOT buyed). Come → came (NOT comed). Write → wrote.
★ Golden Rule: 'I saw it' is correct; 'I seen it' is incorrect without 'have'!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't add -ed to words that already changed: 'went', not 'wented'.

40. Confusables: To / Too / Two
SPaG Essentials
Direction • Also/Excessive • Number
TO: Direction or verb ('Going to school', 'to sleep'). TOO: Means 'also' or 'too much' ('Can I come too?', 'too hot'). TWO: The number 2 ('two tickets').
★ Golden Rule: 'Too' has an extra 'o' because it has too much of something!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'I want to go to' is WRONG — it must be 'I want to go too'.
DfE L1.W40 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
41. There / Their / They're (L1)
SPaG Essentials
Location • Belonging • They Are
THERE has 'here' in it = place ('over there'). THEIR has 'heir' in it = ownership ('their coats'). THEY'RE has an apostrophe = 'they are' ('they're coming').
★ Golden Rule: Test with 'they are' — if it fits, use 'they're'!
⚠️ Watch Out: This is tested in almost every Functional Skills English exam.

42. Essential Level 1 Spellings
SPaG Essentials
The 10 Golden Words
1. Because (Big Elephants Can Always Upset Small Elephants). 2. Beautiful. 3. Believe (never be-LIE-ve a lie). 4. Friend (ends in end). 5. Tomorrow (1 'm', 2 'r's). 6. Wednesday. 7. People.
★ Golden Rule: Spell 'friend' with 'i' before 'e', ending in 'end'!
⚠️ Watch Out: 'Becos' and 'tommorow' are immediate red pen errors.

43. SLC Overview: The Two Assessments
Speaking & Listening
Task 1: Short Talk (4-5m) | Task 2: Group Discussion
Level 1 SLC consists of two parts: (1) A 4–5 minute formal talk or explanation on a prepared topic followed by questions, and (2) A 10–15 minute group discussion on an everyday topic.
★ Golden Rule: Use bullet-point cue cards — never read a full script word-for-word!
⚠️ Watch Out: Reading aloud head-down from an A4 essay script prevents eye contact and caps your grade.

44. Asking Open & Follow-Up Questions
Speaking & Listening
Open Questions (How/Why) vs Closed (Yes/No)
Closed questions (Do you...? Is it...?) get one-word Yes/No answers that stall discussions. Open questions (How would...? Why do you think...?) invite detailed opinions and examples.
★ Golden Rule: Use HOW, WHY, or WHAT to ask open questions and invite full answers!
⚠️ Watch Out: Ask at least two relevant questions to meet the passing criteria.
DfE L1.SLC2 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
45. Turn-Taking & Collaborative Talk
Speaking & Listening
Acknowledge • Build • Invite (A-B-I)
Assessors grade how well you take turns: (1) Acknowledge ("Building on Ana's point..."), (2) Add your evidence, and (3) Invite quieter members ("What is your view on this, David?").
★ Golden Rule: Acknowledge the last speaker before introducing your own point!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never interrupt or dominate — invite quieter group members to speak.
DfE L1.SLC5 • Level 1 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
46. Active Listening & Body Language
Speaking & Listening
Eye Contact • Posture • Measured Pace
Non-verbal communication carries half your impact: maintain steady eye contact across the room, nod to show active listening, speak at a measured pace, and avoid slang in formal talks.
★ Golden Rule: Match your tone and body language to the formality of the setting!
⚠️ Watch Out: Crossing your arms, looking at your phone, or staring only at the assessor loses engagement marks.

Devices & Handling
Tailoring Your Device
Accessibility settings assist users with physical or cognitive impairments: High Contrast Mode (visual clarity), Text Scaling / Magnifier (enlarging text), Screen Reader (Narrator), Sticky Keys (motor support).
★ Golden Rule: Accessibility features ensure digital inclusion for all users!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't confuse display brightness with high-contrast accessibility themes.

2. File Management & Naming
Devices & Handling
Hierarchical Folders & Version Control
Organise files into logical tree hierarchies: Root Folder → Subfolder → Specific file. Meaningful naming convention: Topic_Project_Date_Version (e.g. Budget_Q3_2024_v2.xlsx). Avoid 'Doc1.docx'.
★ Golden Rule: Include the date (YYYY-MM-DD) and version number (v1, v2) in filename!
⚠️ Watch Out: Avoid saving everything to your Desktop — it causes system clutter and data loss risk.

3. File Extensions & Formats
Devices & Handling
Recognising Common File Types
.docx = Word processing. .pdf = Portable read-only document (universal). .xlsx / .csv = Spreadsheets / raw comma-separated data. .pptx = Slideshow. .png / .jpg = Images. .mp4 = Video. .zip = Compressed folder.
★ Golden Rule: Export to PDF before sharing to keep layout and formatting intact!
⚠️ Watch Out: A .csv file saves raw data only — all formulas and styling are lost.

Devices & Handling
Remote Servers & Multi-Device Access
Cloud storage (OneDrive, Google Drive, iCloud) stores files on secure remote servers over the Internet. Benefits: Automatic backup, access from any device, easy real-time collaboration. Requires internet connectivity.
★ Golden Rule: Cloud files protect you against hardware crashes, fires, or stolen laptops!
⚠️ Watch Out: If you don't enable 'Keep on this device' (offline mode), you cannot open cloud files without Wi-Fi.

Devices & Handling
Domains & Sponsored Ads

7. Device Storage vs RAM
Devices & Handling
Storage (SSD/Hard Drive) vs RAM
Storage (GB/TB): Permanent memory holding files and apps when PC is turned off. RAM (Random Access Memory): Temporary working memory used while apps are open. Free up storage by deleting temp files and emptying Recycle Bin.
★ Golden Rule: Empty your Recycle Bin / Trash to permanently reclaim disk storage!
⚠️ Watch Out: Running out of RAM makes your computer freeze; running out of Storage prevents saving new files.

8. Compressing & Extracting (.zip)
Devices & Handling
Reducing File Size for Email
Compress (Zip): Shrinks file size and bundles multiple documents into one single .zip folder for emailing. Extract: Unpacks the zipped files into normal editable documents.
★ Golden Rule: You must EXTRACT files before you can properly edit and save them!
⚠️ Watch Out: If you edit files directly inside an unextracted zip, changes may be lost.

9. Basic Troubleshooting
Devices & Handling
First Steps When Tech Fails
App frozen: Open Task Manager (Ctrl + Shift + Esc) and select 'End Task'. Wi-Fi dropped: Check flight mode, restart router, toggle Wi-Fi off and on. Total system freeze: Hold power button for 10 seconds to reboot.
★ Golden Rule: Restarting clears memory caches — try it first before calling support!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never unplug a PC while it is writing data or installing updates.

10. Data Protection & UK GDPR
Devices & Handling
Handling Personal Data Lawfully
Personal data relates to an identifiable living person (names, NHS numbers, addresses). Under UK GDPR: 1. Process lawfully, fairly, and transparently. 2. Keep accurate and secure. 3. Delete when no longer required.
★ Golden Rule: Always lock your computer screen (Win + L) when leaving your desk!
⚠️ Watch Out: Leaving customer spreadsheets visible on an unattended screen is a serious GDPR data breach.

14. Spreadsheets: Anatomy of a Sheet
Creating Content
Columns, Rows & Cell References
Columns: Lettered vertically (A, B, C...). Rows: Numbered horizontally (1, 2, 3...). Cell Reference: The intersection letter + number (e.g. B4 = column B, row 4). Format cells as Currency (£), Percentage (%), or Date.
★ Golden Rule: Column Letter ALWAYS comes before the Row Number (e.g. C5, NEVER 5C)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Format raw numbers as Currency (£) so the pound sign appears automatically.
DFS 2.4 • Level 1 / 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
15. Spreadsheets: Basic Arithmetic
Creating Content
Always Start with an Equals Sign (=)
Every formula in Excel / Google Sheets MUST begin with '=': Add: =A1+B1. Subtract: =A1-B1. Multiply: =A1*B1 (asterisk). Divide: =A1/B1 (forward slash). Never type hardcoded numbers into formulas.
★ Golden Rule: Always begin spreadsheet formulas with '=' (e.g. =A1+B1)!
⚠️ Watch Out: Use '*' to multiply and '/' to divide — never type the letter 'x'.
DFS 2.5 • Level 1 / 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
16. Spreadsheets: SUM & AVERAGE
Creating Content
Ranges with Colons (e.g. B2:B10)
=SUM(B2:B10): Adds all numbers in range. =AVERAGE(B2:B10): Calculates mean. =MAX(B2:B10): Finds highest value. =MIN(B2:B10): Finds lowest value. Colon (:) means 'through to'.
★ Golden Rule: The colon (:) indicates a contiguous cell range from start to finish!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't write '=SUM(A1+A2)' — either write '=SUM(A1:A2)' or '=A1+A2'.
DFS 2.6 • Level 1 / 2 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
17. Spreadsheets: COUNT vs COUNTA
Creating Content
Count Numbers vs Count Non-Empty Cells
=COUNT(range): Counts ONLY cells containing NUMBERS. =COUNTA(range): Counts ALL non-empty cells (numbers, text, symbols). Think 'Count All' (COUNTA).
★ Golden Rule: Use COUNTA to count attendee names or text entries!
⚠️ Watch Out: If you use COUNT on a column of patient names, the answer will be 0!

50. Copyright & Creative Commons
Safe & Responsible
Intellectual Property, CC Licences & Attribution
Digital media ownership rules: 1. Copyright (©): Automatic legal ownership; you cannot copy or distribute without the author's permission. 2. Creative Commons (CC): Licences allowing free reuse under specific conditions (e.g. CC-BY requires attribution). 3. Public Domain: Free for anyone.

⚠️ Watch Out: Google Image results are NOT automatically free or cleared for use.

1. Place Value up to 1,000
Number System
Hundreds • Tens • Ones (H-T-O)
Every digit in a 3-digit number has a value based on its column: Hundreds (×100), Tens (×10), and Ones (×1). Zero (0) holds an empty column in place.
★ Golden Rule: Read 3-digit numbers from left to right: 407 is Four hundred and seven!
⚠️ Watch Out: Never drop the middle zero: 'Six hundred and five' is 605, NOT 65!
DfE E3.N1 • Entry Level 3 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
2. Column Addition & Subtraction
Number System
Align Right • Start at Ones • Regroup
Always line up Hundreds, Tens, and Ones on the right. Start at the Ones column. In addition, carry 10 to the next column; in subtraction, borrow from the left if the top digit is smaller.
★ Golden Rule: Always start adding or subtracting from the ONES column on the far right!
⚠️ Watch Out: In 342 - 158, do NOT do 8 - 2 = 6! You must borrow 1 ten from the 4 so 12 - 8 = 4.
DfE E3.N2 • Entry Level 3 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
3. Multiplying 2-Digit Numbers
Number System
Partition into Tens & Ones (Grid Method)
To multiply a 2-digit number by a single digit (e.g. 24 × 6), split 24 into 20 and 4. Multiply each part by 6 (20×6 = 120, 4×6 = 24), then add the answers together.
★ Golden Rule: When multiplying by 10, move digits one place left and place a 0 at the end!
⚠️ Watch Out: Don't forget the zero when multiplying the Tens part: 30 × 4 = 120, NOT 12!

4. Division & Interpreting Remainders
Number System
Bus Stop Division • Round Up or Down in Context
Divide from left to right. Any leftover amount is the remainder (r). In real-life problems, decide whether to round UP (e.g. minibuses/boxes needed) or round DOWN (what you can afford).
★ Golden Rule: Round UP when booking seats or buying tins so nothing is left short!
⚠️ Watch Out: If asked for 'full packs', ignore remainder and round DOWN.
DfE E3.N4 • Entry Level 3 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
5. Rounding to Nearest 10 & 100
Number System
5 or More Rounds Up • 4 or Less Stays Same
To round to the nearest 10, look at the Ones digit. To round to the nearest 100, look at the Tens digit. If that neighbour digit is 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, round UP; if 0–4, stay the same.
★ Golden Rule: Use rounded numbers to ESTIMATE and check if your calculator answer is sensible!
⚠️ Watch Out: When rounding 674 to the nearest 100, look at the Tens digit (7), NOT the Ones digit (4)!
DfE E3.N5 • Entry Level 3 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
6. Fractions: Thirds, Quarters, Fifths & Tenths
Number System
Divide by the Bottom • Multiply by the Top
A fraction splits a whole into equal parts. To find a fraction of an amount (e.g. 3/4 of £20): Step 1: Divide the amount by the bottom number (20 ÷ 4 = 5). Step 2: Multiply by the top number (5 × 3 = £15).
★ Golden Rule: Divide by the bottom (denominator), then times by the top (numerator)!
⚠️ Watch Out: 1/3 is BIGGER than 1/5 — a smaller bottom number means larger slices!
DfE E3.N7 • Entry Level 3 Turn over for Practice Challenge ➔ A6 Pocket Card
7. Decimals up to 2 Decimal Places
Number System
Line Up the Decimal Points Vertically
Decimals show tenths (0.1) and hundredths (0.01), just like pounds and pence (£3.45). When adding or subtracting decimals, always line up the decimal points in a straight vertical column.
★ Golden Rule: Add a trailing zero (0.5 = 0.50) so both numbers have 2 decimals!
⚠️ Watch Out: 0.4 is larger than 0.25 because 0.40 has 4 tenths while 0.25 has 2.
